module.title: Counting
module.description: Basic counting (product rule, sum rule, subtraction/inclusion-exclusion), the Pigeonhole Principle, permutations, combinations, and the introductory binomial theorem.

lessons.title: Basic Counting Rules and the Pigeonhole Principle
lessons.welcome: Counting is what we do when we ask 'how many?' This lesson covers the foundational rules — product rule, sum rule, subtraction rule — and the famous Pigeonhole Principle.
objectives: Apply the **product rule** for sequential independent choices.
Apply the **sum rule** for disjoint cases.
Apply the **subtraction rule** (inclusion-exclusion) for overlapping cases.
Recognize counting situations involving Saudi car plates, KAU IDs, and exam choices.

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: When do I multiply and when do I add?

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: Multiply when you make sequential INDEPENDENT choices (product rule): 'choose a shirt AND a pair of shoes'. Add when you have disjoint cases that EXCLUDE each other (sum rule): 'either take a flight OR drive'. If unsure, ask: 'is the count over a single combined choice, or over alternatives?'

flow.title: Product rule
flow.content: If a procedure can be broken into k INDEPENDENT sequential steps, where step i has nᵢ choices, then the total count is `n₁ · n₂ · … · nₖ`.

flow.title: Saudi car plates and KAU IDs
items: **Saudi car plates** are typically 4 digits + 3 letters (Arabic). With 10 digits and (say) 17 allowed Arabic letters: 10⁴ · 17³ = 10000 · 4913 = 49,130,000 possible plates.
**KAU 10-digit student ID:** assuming first digit is fixed at 1 (year prefix) and remaining 9 are free digits: 10⁹ = 1 billion potential IDs.
**Pizza menu:** 3 sizes × 5 sauces × 8 toppings = 120 distinct pizzas.

flow.title: Sum rule
flow.content: If a task can be done in EXACTLY ONE of k disjoint ways, where way i has nᵢ alternatives, the total count is `n₁ + n₂ + … + nₖ`.

flow.title: Subtraction rule (two-set inclusion-exclusion)
flow.content: If a task can be done in n₁ ways OR n₂ ways and the overlap (both at once) has m ways, the count is `n₁ + n₂ − m`.

flow.title: Quick decision
rows: Either case A OR case B (disjoint)
Either case A OR case B (overlapping)

flow.title: Watch for 'OR' that allows both
flow.content: English 'or' is often inclusive. _'Students who took CPCS 203 OR Math 110'_ means at least one — use inclusion-exclusion, not just sum.

flow.title: Pigeonhole Principle
flow.content: If `n + 1` objects are placed into `n` boxes, then at least one box contains **two or more** objects. **Generalized:** if `N` objects are placed into `k` boxes, some box contains at least `⌈N / k⌉` objects.

flow.title: Pigeonhole at KAU
items: **Among 367 students, at least two share a birthday.** 366 possible birthdays + 1 → pigeonhole.
**Among any 13 KAU students, at least two were born in the same month.** 12 months + 1.
**A KAU section of 50 students, 7 lab groups: at least one group has ⌈50/7⌉ = 8 students.**

flow.trigger: After pigeonhole — students often confuse it with probability.

exchange.speaker: Student
exchange.text: Pigeonhole sounds obvious. Why is it useful?

exchange.speaker: Professor
exchange.text: Because it gives a guaranteed conclusion from very little information. We don't need to know anything about the 367 students except their count — pigeonhole forces a shared birthday. It's especially powerful in proofs where we need existence (∃) without construction.

flow.title: Counting passwords
flow.problem: How many 6-character passwords using letters (26 lowercase) and digits (10), where the FIRST character must be a letter?
flow.thinking_process: Apply product rule. Step 1: 26 letters. Steps 2–6: 36 each.
step_by_step_solution: Positions 2–6: each can be any of 26 + 10 = 36 characters.
flow.common_mistake: Treating all 6 positions as letters or as 36 — first position has only 26 options.

flow.title: Sum rule + complement
flow.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 11 Q on either-or counting.
flow.problem: How many integers from 1 to 100 are divisible by 2 or 5?
flow.common_mistake: Forgetting to subtract the overlap (multiples of 10).

flow.title: Pigeonhole
flow.problem: A bag contains red, green, blue socks (many of each). How many socks must you draw to guarantee a matching PAIR?
flow.thinking_process: Worst case: one of each color first.
step_by_step_solution: After 3 draws: could be RGB (one each).
After 4 draws: must repeat a color.
flow.common_mistake: Saying 3 — that allows the worst case of all distinct colors.

flow.title: Common student mistakes
items: Adding when you should multiply (and vice versa).
Using sum rule for overlapping cases — must use inclusion-exclusion.
Forgetting that pigeonhole guarantees existence, not a specific box.
Off-by-one in pigeonhole (need n + 1 not n).

flow.title: Three rules
items: **Product:** AND (independent choices).
**Sum:** OR (disjoint cases).
**Inclusion-exclusion:** OR with overlap.

sections.heading: Pigeonhole Principle
sections.explanation: n+1 items into n boxes forces a duplicate.

sections.heading: Putting them together
sections.explanation: Most counting problems combine multiple rules.

worked_examples.problem: How many 4-digit even integers from 0000 to 9999?
step_by_step_solution: Last digit even: 5 choices. First three: 10·10·10. Total: 5000.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Forgetting that even ends in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8.

quick_checks.question: How many integers from 1 to 30 are divisible by 3 or 5?
Pigeonhole: 13 people, at least 2 share a birth month.

key_takeaways: Product rule for sequential independent choices.
Pigeonhole: n+1 into n forces a duplicate; ⌈N/k⌉ generalized.
summary.next: Next: PERMUTATIONS and COMBINATIONS — counting ordered and unordered selections.

lessons.title: Permutations and Combinations
lessons.welcome: When you select elements from a set, two questions matter: how many to select, and does the ORDER matter? Permutations care about order; combinations do not.
objectives: Define and compute permutations P(n, r) = n!/(n-r)!.
Define and compute combinations C(n, r) = n!/(r!(n-r)!).
Decide whether a problem is a permutation or a combination.

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: How do I tell a permutation from a combination problem?

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: Ask: does the ORDER of selection matter? 'Choose a president, vice-president, and secretary' — order matters (permutation). 'Choose a 3-person committee' — order does not (combination). When in doubt: would (Ahmed, Noura, Sara) and (Sara, Ahmed, Noura) count as different selections? If yes, permutation.

flow.title: Factorial
flow.content: **n!** = n · (n - 1) · (n - 2) · … · 2 · 1, with the convention **0! = 1**. Counts the number of ways to arrange n distinct objects in order.

flow.title: Permutation
flow.content: A **permutation** is an arrangement where order matters. The number of r-permutations of n distinct objects is `P(n, r) = n! / (n - r)! = n · (n-1) · … · (n-r+1)`.

flow.title: Combination
flow.content: A **combination** is a selection where order does NOT matter. The number of r-combinations of n distinct objects is `C(n, r) = n! / (r! · (n - r)!)`. Read 'n choose r'. Always C(n, r) = P(n, r) / r!.

flow.title: Permutation vs combination — which one?
rows: How many ways to seat 4 people in 4 chairs?
How many ways to choose 4 people from 10?
How many ways to pick a president and a vice-president from 10?
How many subsets of {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} have 3 elements?
How many ways to arrange 5 books on a shelf?

flow.title: Counting around campus
items: **KAU lab section of 30 students. Choose a president, a VP, a treasurer.** Order matters (different roles): P(30, 3) = 30·29·28 = 24,360.
**KAU lab section of 30 students. Choose a 3-person committee (no roles).** Order doesn't matter: C(30, 3) = 4,060.
**5 lab partners assigned to 5 lab tables (1 per table).** Permutation: 5! = 120.
**Choose 4 students from 30 for a Saudi Olympiad team.** Combination: C(30, 4) = 27,405.

flow.title: Binomial theorem (introductory)
flow.content: For non-negative integer n: `(x + y)ⁿ = ∑_{r=0}^{n} C(n, r) · x^{n-r} · y^r`. The coefficients C(n, r) are the **binomial coefficients**, also called 'n choose r'.

flow.title: Pascal's triangle (binomial coefficients)
flow.notes: Each entry is the sum of the two above (Pascal's identity: C(n, r) = C(n-1, r-1) + C(n-1, r)).

flow.trigger: After permutation vs combination — students sometimes use the wrong one when the situation has 'arrangement' language.

exchange.speaker: Student
exchange.text: If I choose 5 toppings from 10 to put on a pizza, is order important?

exchange.speaker: Professor
exchange.text: No — pepperoni, mushroom, olives is the same pizza regardless of which topping went on first. Combination: C(10, 5) = 252. Compare with: 'choose 5 lab partners and assign them to lab tables 1, 2, 3, 4, 5' — order matters there: P(10, 5) = 30,240.

flow.title: Permutation
flow.problem: How many ways to arrange the letters of 'KAU' in a row? How many distinct 2-letter strings (no repetition)?
flow.common_mistake: Allowing repetition when the problem says 'no repetition'.

flow.title: Combination
flow.problem: How many 5-card poker hands are there from a standard 52-card deck?
flow.thinking_process: Combination — order of cards in hand doesn't matter.
flow.common_mistake: Computing P(52, 5) — order doesn't matter for poker hands.

flow.title: Mix — combinations + product
flow.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 12 Q on combined counting.
flow.problem: How many committees of 3 men and 2 women can be formed from 5 men and 4 women?
flow.thinking_process: Independent choices: choose men, choose women, multiply.
flow.common_mistake: Adding instead of multiplying — but the choices are independent (each committee selects men AND women).

flow.title: Binomial theorem
flow.thinking_process: Use n = 4 row of Pascal's triangle: 1, 4, 6, 4, 1.
step_by_step_solution: (x + y)⁴ = C(4,0)x⁴ + C(4,1)x³y + C(4,2)x²y² + C(4,3)xy³ + C(4,4)y⁴
flow.common_mistake: Forgetting to subtract powers (x exponent decreases, y increases by 1 each term).

flow.title: Common student mistakes
items: Confusing permutation with combination.
Forgetting 0! = 1.
Allowing repetition when the problem disallows it.
Adding when independent choices require multiplication.

flow.title: Quick decisions
items: **Order matters → permutation P(n, r) = n!/(n-r)!.**
**Order doesn't → combination C(n, r) = n!/(r!(n-r)!).**
**Pascal's identity: C(n, r) = C(n-1, r-1) + C(n-1, r).**

sections.heading: Combinations
sections.explanation: C(n, r) = n!/(r!(n-r)!); order doesn't matter.

key_takeaways: n! arrangements of n distinct objects.

questions.answer: Total = 36⁶. All-letter (no digits) = 26⁶. With at least one digit = 36⁶ - 26⁶ = 2,176,782,336 - 308,915,776 = 1,867,866,560.

questions.answer: Sum: 62⁴ + 62⁵ + 62⁶ + 62⁷ + 62⁸. (Sum rule over disjoint length cases.)

From 10 students, choose 5 with at least 2 specific (Ahmad and Sara) included.
questions.answer: Force Ahmad and Sara in; choose 3 more from remaining 8: C(8, 3) = 56.

questions.question: Pigeonhole: how many cards must you draw from a standard 52-card deck to guarantee 4 of the same suit?
questions.answer: Worst: 3 of each suit = 12 cards. Next draw must give a 4th of some suit. So 13 cards.
